name: Apache

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Chiricahua imprisonment and the limits of the archive
claimBlocks.text: The 2010 Chiricahua assessment follows removal and imprisonment through Florida, Alabama and Oklahoma, including the separation of children for schooling. Its introduction warns that historical timelines inherit the priorities of predominantly non-Apache records. Reading the narrative with that warning helps distinguish administrative decisions from Apache experiences. The work concerns particular Chiricahua histories; its account cannot serve as a single chronology for every Apache people or erase later community relationships.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Schooling on White Mountain Apache land
claimBlocks.text: Welch’s 2011 nomination connects Fort Apache’s military history with its conversion to the Theodore Roosevelt School. It describes a federal assimilation project, initially enrolling Navajo and Hopi children, while local Apache families sought education closer to home. The resulting disputes concerned whose children the institution served and who directed its purposes. This local history shows why a school on Apache land cannot simply be assumed to have enrolled only Apache children.

An 1887 Senate document collects official correspondence about schooling for Apache prisoners at Fort Marion. It reports transfers to Carlisle and records a contract for teaching younger children in St. Augustine. Letters also discuss efforts to obtain parents’ agreement. These administrative voices reveal arrangements made within a system of captivity; they do not independently establish freely given consent, children’s own experiences or the officials’ claims about adequate care.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Printed/PDF 1–5, especially transmittal 1 and Pratt correspondence 4–5

inspections.method: Actual PDF reader supplied title/imprint, contents, selected introductory passages and historical narrative. Download attempt with ordinary TLS validation failed and was not bypassed. No local full-report file or image QA claimed.
inspections.readingDetails: Printed 3–4 and 6–7 correspond to PDF 12–13 and 15–16; printed 245–249 correspond to PDF 254–258. Historical narrative attribution is to the selected chapter authors, not silently to every cited historian or Apache participant.
inspections.limits: Avoiding exact removal counts, deaths, demographic statistics, private locations, ceremonial descriptions, medical/ethnobotanical instructions and reburial material. A reference to September1885 in a captivity passage appears inconsistent with the surrounding1886narrative; this exact chronology is not adopted. The companion film remains unviewed and has separate tribal copyright restrictions; no film content/media reproduced.

distinctWorkNotes: The NPS2010assessment is one compilation; chapter-five narrative, introduction, timeline and bibliography do not become separate sources.
The2011nomination is one work, distinct from the2010Chiricahua assessment in authorship, subject and documentary purpose. A related SAH Archipedia entry was not obtained and adds no separate count.
The1887Senate compilation is an original historical work, distinct from later secondary syntheses. Its individual letters/contracts and GovInfo metadata/PDF manifestations do not inflate the count.

No source is a duplicate of the San Carlos/Yavapai/Tonto community webpage renewals. Overlapping historical subjects with another packet must still be deduplicated if the same work is discovered under another URL.
identityAndDateNotes: Chiricahua histories and forced movement through multiple places do not describe all Western, Plains, Jicarilla, Lipan or Mescalero experiences.

White Mountain Apache land, a federal boarding school, its diverse pupils and present tribal institutions are related subjects with different scopes. Initial Navajo/Hopi attendance must not be recast as all-Apache attendance.

2010report imprint,2011nomination preparation/editorial dates,2012host path and1887ordered-printing date have different meanings. No present operation, legal jurisdiction or unchanged government arrangement is inferred.
Historical administrative vocabulary is source evidence of colonial priorities, not vocabulary to adopt uncritically in the profile’s own description.

excludedAndUnread.title: Underlying archival reports, scholarly books and the assessment’s companion tribal film
excludedAndUnread.status: Citations and descriptions encountered within inspected works do not constitute original inspection. No separate counts or media rights inferred.

researchGaps: The assessment’s historical chronology contains at least one apparent inconsistency; precise event dating should be compared with original records before adding a detailed timeline.

The archival compilation lacks an unmediated parent/child viewpoint in the selected pages. Further public community-authored testimony could help balance official accounts without publishing sensitive narratives.
No full-volume review, current boarding-school operation/outcome audit, current legal advice or comprehensive history of every Apache community is claimed.
